issues.legal_issue: A state procedure requiring a tenant to deposit admitted rent during a pending rent-recovery suit is not invalid merely because of a later central amendment to the civil procedure code when the central amendment does not occupy the same field.
material_facts: The suits sought arrears of rent, or rent and possession, and the tenants’ defences were struck off for failure to comply with the state procedure requiring deposits of admitted rent.
The state procedure added a rule governing rent deposits during such suits; the central amendment amended a different rule and did not address the state rule’s subject matter.
The central amendment was made before the later state amendment took effect, but the state amendment had received presidential assent.
issues.conclusion: The state rule remained valid and was not repealed or rendered void by repugnancy.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 254(1) and (2) of the Constitution and Section 97(1) of the central amending Act, repugnancy requires inconsistent provisions that occupy the same field and cannot operate together; the making of the laws, rather than their respective commencement dates, is relevant to their priority. A state law that conflicts with an earlier central law may prevail in the state if it is reserved for and receives presidential assent, subject to Parliament’s later power to legislate. The Court applied the principles in Zaverbhai Amaidas v. State of Bombay, Ch. Tika Ramji v. State of U.P., Deep Chand v. State of Uttar Pradesh, M. Karunanidhi v. Union of India, Krishna District Cooperative Marketing Society Ltd. v. N.V. Pumachandra Rao, and Gauri Shankar Gaur v. State of U.P.; it distinguished Ganpat Giri v. II Additional District Judge because that case concerned a state amendment to a rule that the central amendment had replaced with a complete provision. The central amendment was an amending, not consolidating and repealing, enactment; the code itself also permitted striking a defence in specified circumstances.

predicates.rent_recovery_suit: A landlord brought a civil suit seeking rent arrears, rent, or possession from a tenant.
predicates.state_rule_requires_ongoing_rent_deposit: A state rule required a tenant to deposit admitted rent during the continuing suit and permitted the court to strike the defence for default.
predicates.central_amendment_does_not_cover_same_fi: The central amendment did not amend or otherwise govern the procedure addressed by the state rule.

issues.definition: When a rent-recovery suit is governed by a state rule requiring ongoing rent deposits and the central amendment does not cover that same procedural field, the state procedure remains valid.

issues.legal_issue: A procedure that permits striking a tenant’s defence for failing to deposit admitted rent does not violate equality merely because tenants in different procedural positions are treated differently.
material_facts: The procedure applied to tenants who defaulted in paying admitted rent during a rent suit and allowed the court to consider a timely representation before striking the defence.
A tenant who made a bona fide mistake could receive discretionary relief in light of prior conduct and mitigating circumstances.
Tenants who disputed the tenancy or rent were in a different position from tenants who failed to pay admitted rent after a court order; tenants within the latter class were treated alike.
issues.conclusion: The procedure was not discriminatory, arbitrary, or capricious and did not violate Article 14.
issues.legal_principle: Article 14 permits classification based on an intelligible differentia with a rational connection to the legislative purpose. The Court held that the separate treatment of tenants seeking relief for a bona fide initial mistake, tenants disputing the tenancy, and tenants who defaulted on admitted rent after an order was justified. The procedure aimed to reduce landlords’ hardship and prevent delay in rent suits; the distinct relief available under Section 20(4) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of Letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972, did not make the procedures discriminatory.

predicates.small_causes_rent_suit: A landlord brought a rent or possession suit in a court empowered to hear small causes.
predicates.tenant_defaulted_on_admitted_rent_after_: The tenant failed to pay admitted rent after the court required continued payment as a condition of contesting the suit.
predicates.defaulting_tenants_are_treated_alike: Tenants who defaulted in the same relevant circumstances were subject to the same procedure.
predicates.tenant_groups_have_distinct_procedural_p: The tenants subject to the procedure differed in relevant ways from tenants who sought relief for an initial mistake or disputed the tenancy or rent.

issues.definition: If a tenant in a small-causes rent suit defaults on admitted rent after a court order, and the procedure treats similarly situated defaulting tenants alike while distinguishing tenants in materially different procedural positions, the procedure does not violate equality.

issues.legal_issue: A statutory amendment that expressly applies to pending proceedings applies to those proceedings even when the relevant right or cause of action arose before the amendment.
material_facts: The rent suits were pending when the central amending Act took effect.
Section 97(3) stated that the amended principal Act applied to pending suits and proceedings notwithstanding that the relevant right or cause of action had accrued earlier.
issues.conclusion: The amended provisions applied retrospectively to pending proceedings, including proceedings instituted before the relevant state and central amendments took effect.
issues.legal_principle: Section 97(3) expressly applies the principal Act as amended to pending suits, proceedings, appeals, and applications notwithstanding the earlier accrual of the right or cause of action. The Court held that this language gives the amendment retrospective operation and affects vested rights to that extent.

predicates.civil_proceeding_pending_when_amendment_: A civil suit or other civil proceeding remained pending when the amendment took effect.
predicates.amendment_expressly_covers_pending_proce: The amendment states that it applies to pending proceedings even if the underlying right or cause of action arose earlier.

issues.definition: If a civil proceeding is pending when an amendment takes effect and the amendment expressly covers pending proceedings despite earlier accrual, the amended procedure applies to that proceeding.
